content.title: About
content.content: Fufu is a traditional dish made from boiled and pounded starchy root vegetables (commonly cassava, yam or plantain), popular across West and Central Africa. It has a soft, slightly sticky texture and a neutral flavor, making it a versatile base for soups, stews and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fufu is traditionally prepared by hand, pounding the cooked root in a large wooden mortar.
There are many regional variations: Nigeria uses yam, Ghana prefers cassava, Cameroon often uses plantain.
It is typically served in small balls that are picked up with the fingers and dipped into sauce.
The dish is considered a symbol of hospitality and family tradition.
In some cultures fufu is called “the food of strength,” providing energy for hard labor.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Fufu provides slowly digestible carbs that give sustained energy and promote satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Traditional fufu contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: The root vegetables used in fufu supply fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Depending on the base ingredient, fufu can provide vitamin C, potassium and magnesium.

items.title: Hypoallergenic
items.content: For most people fufu does not trigger allergies, as it is free from nuts, gluten and dairy.

items.title: Cyanogenic compounds
items.content: Some varieties of raw cassava contain cyanogenic glycosides that can be toxic if not properly cooked.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Fufu can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar, so individuals with diabetes should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Potential contamination
items.content: Improper storage of the raw roots can lead to mold or bacterial growth, making the product unsafe.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fufu is usually served hot, shaped into small balls that are picked up with the fingers and dipped into meat, fish or vegetable sauces. It can also be used as a base for casseroles or added to soups as a thickener.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh roots (cassava, yam, plantain) in a cool, dry place or refrigerate for up to 3–5 days. Cooked fufu keeps in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days; for longer storage freeze in portion‑size bags.
